of the stake within the territorial reach of the court. In NEW YORK LIFE INS. CO. v. DUNLEVY, 241 U.S. 518, 36 S.Ct. 613, 60 L.Ed.
1140 (1916), the Supreme Court was faced with the question whether to treat a debt as an in rem or quasi in rem basis for interpleader,
and held that the interpleader was an in personam proceeding requiring personal service on the claimants before they could be bound by
the judgment. As commentary explains:
The Dunlevy decision had the effect of rendering interpleader unavailable in the federal courts in most cases in which the claimants were of
diverse citizenship. In the absence of a federal statute extending the jurisdictional reach of the district courts in interpleader actions, the
prevailing territorial limitations on personal jurisdiction effectively barred the courts from offering relief when one of the claimants was
from a state other than the forum. As a result, businesses engaged in interstate commerce that were confronted by conflicting claims to a
particular fund often found themselves unavoidably defending several suits in different states. The situation was particularly troublesome for
insurance companies due to the frequency with which multiple claims to the proceeds of an insurance policy arose.
7 Wright, Miller & Kane, Federal Practice and Procedure § 1701 (3d ed.). Congress responded to the problem in 1917 with the enactment of the first
federal interpleader statute.
3.INTERPLEADER IN THE FEDERAL COURTS
———
Reread 28 U.S.C. §§ 1335, 1397, and 2361 and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 22 in the Supplement.
———
The 1917 Federal Interpleader Act was successively broadened in 1926 and 1936 and was reconstituted in 1948 as part of the United
States Judicial Code. The present Interpleader Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1335, 1397, and 2361, manifests a congressional intent to avoid a
repetition of the Dunlevy decision in a federal court. Section 1397 permits venue to be laid in any judicial district in which at least one of
the claimants resides and Section 2361 permits nationwide service of process in order to reach all of the claimants. Further recognition of
the interstate quality of interpleader and the need for the exercise of federal judicial power in this context is the provision in 28 U.S.C.

§ 1335 permitting the federal courts to assert jurisdiction when the stake is worth as little as $500 (the property is deposited into the court
registry) and there is diversity of citizenship between or among “[t]wo or more adverse claimants.” The federal statutes on interpleader are
